title: The Entire History Of Artificial Intelligence Explained Slowly (For Sleep)
fullText: Hello and welcome. You have found a quiet place, a soft landing at the end of a long day. And I am glad you are here. Wherever you are lying right now, whatever surface is holding your weight, let it hold you just a little more completely. Feel the places where your body meets the bed, the pillow, the blanket. You do not need to adjust anything or fix your position or make anything happen. You have already done enough today. The only thing left to do is to let go of the day piece by piece and allow the sound of a calm voice to carry you somewhere gentle and undemanding. Tonight, if you would like, I am going to tell you a story. It is a long story and a slow one, and there is no rush to get through it. The story is about machines that think. Or more carefully, it is about the long human effort to build machines that might one day think, or something like thinking, and the many turns that effort has taken across centuries and decades. But that makes it sound grand and complicated. And it is not meant to feel that way tonight. Tonight, it is simply a thread to follow, a path to walk in your mind while your body sinks deeper into rest. You do not need to pay close attention. You do not need to remember any names or dates or ideas. If you drift away for a while and then drift back, the story will still be here, moving along at the same unhurried pace, and you will not have missed anything that cannot be gently gathered up again. Think of this as sitting by a very slow river, watching the water move past. Sometimes you notice the shape of a particular ripple or the way the light falls on the surface and sometimes your eyes close and you simply hear the sound of the water without tracking any single detail. Both ways of being with the river are perfectly fine. The river does not mind if you doze. In the same way, this story does not ask for your focus. It offers itself to you like a blanket you can pull up or push away as you like. There is no test at the end, no point you must carry forward, nothing you will be asked to recall tomorrow. The only thing this story wants to do is to be beside you for a little while, a quiet companion in the dark and then to fade softly as sleep arrives. So let us begin with the simplest version of what we are talking about when we talk about machines that think. For as long as people have been people, they have looked at the world and wondered if the things they made could ever come alive, could ever act with purpose, could ever seem to have a mind of their own. This wondering is very old. It appears in stories carved into stone, in myths passed down around fires, in the daydreams of inventors long before the word computer ever existed. The story we are going to walk through tonight starts in that ancient wondering and moves forward step by slow step through real events and real people and real machines all the way to the tools that sit on desks and in pockets today. But that is the whole shape of the journey and we are not going to rush toward the end. We are going to take our time. The story moves from old dreams of thinking objects to the first careful attempts to write down the rules of logic. It moves from there to the earliest calculating machines built of brass and steel and cranked by hand. It moves to a man sitting in an English garden during a world war imagining a test that might tell us whether a machine could truly be said to think. It moves to a summer workshop in a small New Hampshire town where a group of young researchers gave the whole endeavor a name. From there, the story rises and falls like breath, like the tide. There were seasons of great hope when people believed that machines with human-like intelligence were just a few years away. And there were seasons of disappointment when the money dried up and the big promises did not come true. And the whole field seemed to go quiet. Those quiet seasons have a name that some historians use. They are called winters, artificial intelligence winters, long cold stretches when progress seemed to stop. But even in the winters, work continued in small rooms and quiet labs. And when the seasons turned again, new ideas began to grow. The story will take us through those seasons and through the rise of machines that could play chess and answer quiz show questions and recognize a face in a photograph. It will take us right up to the present moment where the tools are changing very quickly and many questions remain wide open. And through all of it, I will try to speak slowly and clearly and without any rush. If a word or an idea sounds unfamiliar, I will explain it in plain language before I use it again. If a number or a date matters, I will say it out in full words, so your mind does not have to translate a symbol into meaning. Everything here is designed to be easy on a tired mind, a mind that is already halfway to sleep and does not need any new puzzles to solve. So let yourself settle. Let your breathing find its own natural rhythm. You do not need to control it or deepen it or change it in any way. Just notice the air moving in and out and let the noticing itself be soft and light like a hand resting on a sleeping cat. There is nothing urgent here. There is nothing to accomplish. The whole of this story is a gift you can receive or not receive and it will not be offended either way. I want to say one more thing before we step into the oldest part of the story. The subject of machines that think can sometimes stir up strong feelings. People worry about what these tools might mean for jobs, for art, for what it means to be human. Those are real and serious questions, but they are not questions we need to wrestle with tonight. Tonight we are simply telling a story, a long historical story, and we are telling it in the calmst way we know how. If any part of the story touches on something that feels heavy or worrisome, you can let that weight go. You can set it down beside the bed. It will still be there in the morning if you want to pick it up again. But for now, in the dark, with the sound of a slow voice in your ears, you do not need to carry anything at all. The story begins as many old stories do in the ancient world. Before there were computers, before there were engines, before there was even the idea of a machine that could calculate, there were myths and legends about objects that seemed to move and act as if they were alive. These were not real machines in the way we understand machines now. They were stories. But stories are where human imagination does its first work, sketching out possibilities long before anyone has the tools to build them. The ancient Greeks told tales of a bronze giant named Talos, who was said to guard the island of Cree by striding around its coastline three times each day, hurling rocks at any ship that came too near. Talos was not a god and not a man. He was something in between, a thing made by a god, but built of metal with a single vein of molten lead running through him, sealed with a bronze pin at his ankle. The stories say that Talos was made by Hephestus, the god of fire and metal work and craft. Hephest appears again and again in these old myths as the maker of things that moved. He was said to have built golden handmaidadens who could walk and speak and carry things for him and mechanical tripods that rolled on their own to and from the feasts of the gods. These were not living beings in the way a person is alive. But they were not simply statues either. They occupied a middle space in the imagination, a space where crafted matter took on the appearance of will. These stories are not history in the factual sense. No bronze giant ever walked around Cree. No golden handmaiden ever spoke. But the stories matter because they show us something about the human mind. They show us that the desire to make things that act alive is very deep and very old. It predates electricity. It predates steam. It predates the written word for engine. It is a desire that seems to come with the shape of the human brain itself. the urge to see our own reflection in the things we build, to make objects that move and respond and seem to have purpose. That urge sat quietly in the human imagination for thousands of years, expressing itself in myths and legends and later in clockwork until the mathematics and the machinery finally caught up with the dream. We will come to that mathematics soon enough. But for now, in these first quiet minutes together, I want you simply to picture an ancient coastline, the Agian Sea, dark and wrinkled under a low sky, and a huge bronze figure moving slowly along the rocks, patient and tireless, asking nothing, needing nothing, doing only what it was made to do. This image is not a fact. It is a dream, but it is the first dream in our story, and it is a good place to start. Let the image rest in your mind if you like, or let it go. Either is fine. The story will wait for you. It is not in a hurry. And you, wherever you are, are exactly where you need to be. Let your eyes stay closed. Let your breathing stay slow. We have all the time we need. The story continues when you are ready. And if you fall asleep before it goes any further, then the story has done its work, and I could not be more glad. The dream of making something that moves on its own, that acts as if it has purpose, that seems in some way alive, is a very old dream. It is older than the written word for machine. Older than the first gears carved from wood, older than the first smith who learned to pour molten bronze into a mold. Long before anyone could build a thinking thing, people told stories about them. And those stories passed down around fires and carved into stone and later written onto scrolls are where our slow journey truly begins. The ancient Greeks, who lived around the Aian Sea more than 2,000 years ago, told many tales of objects that moved and acted as if they had minds. The most vivid of these tales is the story of Talos. Talos was a giant made of bronze, a towering figure crafted not by human hands, but by a god. The god was Hephestus, the smith of the Olympians, the one who worked with fire and metal in a great forge beneath a mountain. Ephesus made many wondrous things in the old stories. He made shields that gleamed like the sun. He made a throne that trapped the person who sat in it, and he made Talos, the bronze guardian of Cree. According to the myth, Talos walked around the entire island of Cree three times each day, scanning the horizon for ships that might bring invaders. When he saw a threat, he would tear huge rocks from the cliffs and hurl them into the sea, driving the ships away. Inside his bronze body ran a single vein of molten lead sealed with a bronze pin at his ankle. In some versions of the story, a sorceress named Medadia tricked him and pulled the pin and the molten life of him poured out onto the ground. Now, no one alive today believes that a real bronze giant once walked around Cree. This is a myth, a story, a piece of imagination. But the details of the story tell us something important about the human mind. The people who told the story of Talos were picturing something that did not exist and could not exist with their technology. They were picturing a crafted object, a made thing that could move on its own, make decisions about threats, patrol a border, carry out a purpose. They were in a way imagining a robot 3,000 years before the word robot was invented. Talos was not alive in the way a person is alive. He had no soul, no feelings, no inner life that the stories mention. He was simply a machine made of bronze set to a task and he did that task without rest or complaint. The story does not ask us to love Talos or to fear him exactly. It simply presents him as a fact of that imagined world, a thing that existed between the category of statue and the category of living being. Hephestus himself appears throughout Greek myth as the maker of things that blur this same boundary. In one story, he builds a set of golden handmaidaidens who attend him in his forge. These handmaidaidens are described as being made of gold and they can move and they can speak and they possess intelligence enough to help him with his work. In another story, he builds mechanical tripods that roll on their own to the feasts of the gods and then roll back again when the feast is done. These tripods do not speak and do not think. They simply move back and forth performing their one task. But to the people who first told these stories, the idea of a self-moving object was clearly a source of wonder. It was a thing worth describing, worth passing down, worth carving into the marble freezes of temples. The urge to imagine objects that act alive was not a small or rare thing. It was woven deeply into the way the ancient Greeks thought about craft and skill and the power of making. If you let your mind drift a little, you can picture these early dreamers. You can see a storyteller standing in a courtyard in the early evening, the sky going orange and purple over the sea, a small crowd gathered around. The storyteller describes the great smith god at his forge, the glow of the fire on his face, the golden handmaidaidens moving smoothly across the stone floor, their metal feet making a soft ringing sound. The listeners lean in. They know this is not real in the ordinary sense. They know no such golden women exist in the world. But the image is powerful. It stays with them. They carry it home. And later they tell it to their children. And the children grow up and tell it to their own children. The dream passes from mind to mind across many lifetimes, waiting for the day when the tools and the knowledge might catch up. Now dreams and myths are one thing, and built objects are another. But there came a time many centuries after the ancient Greeks when skilled craftsmen began to make real moving figures not out of myth but out of metal and wood and clockwork. These were not thinking machines in any real sense. They were mechanical automatter figures that could perform a set of motions often powered by springs or weights or water. They did not decide anything. They did not learn. They simply repeated the same movements over and over, like a music box playing its one tune. But to the people who saw them, they could feel uncanny, as if something like life had been captured in brass and steel. During the medieval period and the Renaissance in Europe, skilled clock makers and metal workers built automata for royal courts and wealthy patrons. These were often figures of people or animals that could move in simple ways. A clockwork monk might walk across a table and raise across. A mechanical lion might rear up on its hind legs and roar. A silver swan might dip its neck and appear to drink from a flowing stream of glass beads. These objects were extremely expensive to make. They required hundreds of tiny gears and levers, all cut and fitted by hand, often over years of patient labor. They were not built for any practical purpose. They were built to delight and to impress, to show that the person who owned them was powerful enough to command such wonders. They were a kind of magic that was not magic, a demonstration of human skill pushed to its furthest edge. One of the most famous builders of automata was a Frenchman named Jacqu Devokans who lived in the 18th century. In 1737, when he was still a young man, he completed a mechanical duck that became famous across Europe. The duck was life-sized, made of gilded copper, and it could perform a series of remarkably lifelike actions. It could stand up, sit down, stretch its neck, flap its wings, and quack. But the detail that most astonished people was that the duck appeared to eat and digest. A person could place a few grains of grain into the duck's beak and the duck would swallow them and a moment later a little pellet would emerge from the other end. Vulcans claimed that the duck had a small chemical laboratory in its stomach that broke the grain down. But this was not true. The duck actually had a hidden compartment containing pre-made pellets that were released at the right moment. The eating and digesting were a clever illusion, not a real biological process. Still, the duck was a marvel. People lined up to see it. They paid money to watch a mechanical bird do what a real bird does. Vocans himself went on to build other automata, including a flute player that actually played a flute, using a system of bellows and levers to move air through the instrument. But he is best remembered for the duck, because the duck captured something about the human imagination. It was not alive, and everyone knew it was not alive. But it acted alive in a way that was just convincing enough to blur the line for a moment to make the viewer feel that strange mix of recognition and strangeness that comes from seeing a made thing imitate a living thing. Now there is an important distinction to draw here and it is worth drawing slowly so that it settles clearly. All of the automata we have been describing, from the golden handmaidaidens of myth to the clockwork duck of Vcons, were objects that moved. They imitated the outward appearance of life. They did not think, even in the simplest sense. They followed a fixed mechanical path, like a clock hand moving around a dial. What makes a clock tick is a spring unwinding or a weight descending, not a decision. What made the duck appear to eat was a set of gears and levers arranged in advance by Vconson, not any kind of recognition of the grain. The duck did not know it was eating. It did not know anything at all. It was a beautiful machine, but it was only a machine. The story we are following tonight is about something different. It is about the effort to build machines that do not only move but seem to think. Machines that can solve problems, learn from examples, recognize patterns, make choices. That effort required something that automata did not require. It required a way of thinking about thinking itself, a way of describing reasoning as a kind of step-by-step process. It required the insight that logic could be written down as a set of simple operations and that those operations could be carried out not by a mind but by a machine. That insight was not going to come from clockwork. It was going to come from mathematics. But the old dreams of thinking things are not separate from the later mathematics. They are the soil in which the later ideas grew. The human mind across centuries kept returning to the same question. Can we make something that acts like us? Can we make something that seems to have a will of its own? The ancient Greeks asked it in myth. The medieval craftsman asked it in clockwork. Vocon asked it in his gilded duck. The question never went away. Even when the tools to answer it did not yet exist. It was passed down in stories and in craft traditions from one generation to the next. And when the mathematics finally arrived in the quiet work of a few lonely thinkers in the 19th century, it arrived into a world that had been dreaming of thinking machines for a very long time. So as we leave the old dreams behind and begin to move toward the paper and the numbers and the formal logic, it is good to remember that the impulse did not start with logic. It started with wonder. It started with the sight of a bronze giant in a story striding along a rocky coast under a wide dark sky. It started with the image of a golden handmaiden speaking in a god's forge. It started with the strange, lovely, slightly eerie motion of a clockwork duck stretching its neck toward a handful of grain. These things were not artificial intelligence. They were not even attempts at artificial intelligence. They were simply the early expressions of a very old human curiosity. The curiosity about whether the things we make might one day share in something we recognize as life. Let that curiosity rest in your mind for a moment. Let it settle there softly like a feather landing on still water. The story is about to shift. We are going to leave the realm of myth and clockwork and enter the realm of symbols and equations. But the shift is gentle. It is not a break. It is more like a river rounding a slow bend, changing its view, but not its nature. The water is the same water. The current is the same current. And you floating along with it do not need to do anything but drift. Your breathing can stay slow. Your eyes can stay closed. The story will carry you forward into the quiet into the next part of the night where a man with a quill pen is about to write down the first rules of thought itself. The shift from dreams to something more solid did not happen all at once. It happened slowly over decades in the quiet work of a handful of people who were asking a new kind of question. Not can we make a thing that moves like a living creature but can we make a thing that follows the rules of thought itself. This was a question about logic about the shape of reasoning about whether the act of thinking could be broken down into steps so small and so clear that even a machine with no mind at all could carry them out. And the first person to make real progress on this question was not an engineer or an inventor in the usual sense. He was a mathematician, a quiet man living in England in the middle of the 19th century and his name was George Bool. George B was born in the city of Lincoln in 1815. The son of a shoemaker, he did not come from money or status. He taught himself mathematics by reading books in his spare time and eventually he became a professor at Queens College in Cork, Ireland. In 1854, he published a book with a long and careful title. It was called an investigation of the laws of thought on which are founded the mathematical theories of logic and probabilities. The title was a mouthful, but the idea inside was elegant and surprisingly simple. Bull had found a way to write down the process of logical reasoning using nothing more than the values true and false which he represented as the numbers one and zero. Think about what that means for a moment. When a person reasons about something, they are often moving through a series of small decisions. Is it raining? If it is raining, then I will bring an umbrella. If it is not raining, then I will leave the umbrella at home. Each of these small decisions is a kind of fork in the path. A moment where the answer is either yes or no, true or false. Ble showed that you could write these forks down using a very small set of simple operations. You could combine true and false values using words like and, or, and not. For example, you might say, "It is raining and it is cold," which is true only if both things are true at the same time. Or you might say, "It is raining or it is cold," which is true if at least one of them is true. Or you might say, "It is not raining," which simply flips the truth value around. These three little words and, or, and, not, turned out to be enough to describe an enormous range of logical reasoning. This system of working with true and false values is now called Boolean logic after Bool himself. But the name is less important than the idea. The idea is that reasoning can be treated as a kind of arithmetic. Just as you can add and subtract numbers, you can combine true and false values and get a definite predictable result. And if reasoning can be treated as arithmetic, then a machine that can do arithmetic might in principle be able to do some forms of reasoning. Ble himself did not build such a machine. He was a mathematician working with pen and paper. But his work opened a door. It showed that logic was not a misty mysterious thing that only human minds could touch. It was a system with rules and rules can be written down. and anything that can be written down can in theory be given to a machine. Now, at roughly the same time that Bool was working out the laws of thought, another Englishman was dreaming of a machine that could carry out calculations of any kind. His name was Charles Babage, and he was a man of large ideas and difficult personality, someone who spent much of his life designing machines that were never finished. Babage was born in 1791 and he grew up in a world where calculation was done by hand often with the help of printed tables of numbers. These tables were used for navigation, for astronomy, for engineering, and they were full of errors because they were copied and recomputed by human beings who made mistakes. Babage wanted to build a machine that could calculate these tables automatically without error driven by gears and cranks and steam. His first design was called the difference engine and it was meant to compute mathematical tables using a method of repeated addition. He built a small working model but the full machine was never completed. The British government gave him money and he spent years on it. But the engineering of the time was not precise enough and Babage kept changing his designs and eventually the project stalled. But while he was working on the difference engine, a larger and more remarkable idea began to form in his mind. He imagined a machine that was not limited to one kind of calculation. He imagined a machine that could be given instructions, that could read those instructions from punched cards, that could store numbers in a kind of memory, and that could perform any sequence of mathematical operations. He called this imagined machine the analytical engine. The analytical engine was never built, not even a small part of it. Babbage drew hundreds of detailed plans, and he talked about it endlessly to anyone who would listen. But the money and the political will and the manufacturing skill were not there. The machine existed only on paper, but on paper it was a remarkable thing. It had a section called the mill, which is where the arithmetic would happen, and a section called the store, which is where numbers would be held until they were needed. This division between a place for processing and a place for memory is in a very basic way the same division that exists in every modern computer. Babage did not have electronics. He had brass and steel and steam power. But the logical structure he imagined was far ahead of its time. And here is where another figure enters the story. A woman whose name has been remembered and debated and celebrated in different ways across the years. Her name was Ada Love Lace. She was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, though she never knew him and she was raised by her mother to study mathematics, which was unusual for a woman of her class in that era. She met Charles Babage when she was a young woman, and she became deeply interested in his analytical engine. In 1842 and 1843, she translated a paper about the engine that had been written in French by an Italian mathematician named Luigi Menabraa. But she did more than just translate it. She added her own notes which ran to several times the length of the original paper. And in those notes, she wrote things that no one else had quite written before. Love Lace understood that the analytical engine was not just a number cruncher. She saw that it could work with symbols of any kind, not just numbers, as long as the rules for manipulating those symbols could be written down clearly. She wrote that the engine might one day compose music or create patterns or work with abstract ideas. She understood that the machine was a generalpurpose device, something that could follow any set of rules given to it. and she wrote what is now considered the first published description of a step-by-step sequence of operations designed to be carried out by such a machine. In other words, she wrote what many people now think of as the first computer program, even though the machine it was written for did not exist. It is important to be calm and clear about what Love Lace did and did not do. She did not build a working machine. She did not invent the analytical engine. Her notes were speculative, not a report on something that had been tested. The program she wrote was never run because there was no engine to run it on. But her insight was genuine, and it was deep. She saw perhaps more clearly than Babage himself, that a machine that could manipulate symbols according to rules was not limited to arithmetic. It could in theory work with anything that could be expressed symbolically, music, images, language, logic. This was a huge leap of imagination, and it pointed directly toward the idea of a thinking machine, even though Love Lace herself was careful not to claim too much. In her notes, she wrote that the analytical engine had no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It could only do what it was told to do. It could follow rules, but it could not make them up. That distinction between following rules and originating ideas is a distinction that will echo through the rest of this story. It is the question at the heart of everything that comes later. Can a machine that only follows rules ever be said to think? Or is thinking something more than rule following? Love Lace did not try to answer that question. She simply described what the machine could do and left the deeper questions for others. But by describing what the machine could do so clearly, she helped lay the foundation for those deeper questions to be asked. Now, it is worth pausing here to notice something about the pace of this story. Between Bull's logic in 1854 and Love Lace's notes in 1843, we are talking about ideas that sat on paper for decades, sometimes for a century, before the technology existed to build machines that could put them into practice. The 19th century was full of brilliant theoretical work that had to wait. The world did not yet have electricity in common use. It did not have vacuum tubes or transistors or silicon chips. It had steam and clockwork and paper and ink. The people who were thinking about the laws of thought were thinking far ahead of what anyone could build. They were planting seeds in ground that was not yet ready for them. But the seeds did not die. They waited, preserved in libraries and mathematical journals, and they were ready when the technology finally began to catch up. You can picture these early thinkers if you like as you lie there in the dark. Picture George Bool at his desk in Cork, writing out his true and false equations by candle light. The window dark, the house quiet, the only sound the scratching of his pen. Picture Charles Babage in his London workshop, surrounded by half-finished brass gears and drawings on rolls of paper, arguing with his machinists, firing off letters to the government, asking for more money. His great engine still just out of reach. Picture Ada Love Lace, a young woman in a stiff Victorian dress, sitting with paper and ink, thinking her way into a machine that did not exist, seeing further into its possibilities than almost anyone around her. These were not people building robots. They were people building ideas, piece by careful piece. And those ideas are still with us now, still running underneath all the technology we use every day. The story of machines that think is not only a story of hardware. It is at its deepest level a story of ideas about what thinking is and whether it can be captured in rules. Ble showed that some kinds of reasoning can be captured in rules. Babbage designed a machine that could follow rules. Love lace saw that such a machine could follow rules about anything, not just numbers. Together they established the logical and mechanical possibility of a thinking machine. Even though no such machine yet existed, they left the question hanging in the air, waiting for the 20th century to pick it up. And the 20th century did pick it up. The next part of our story belongs to a man who took these ideas and pushed them further into the realm of actual computing machines and into the deepest question of all. Can a machine be said to think? But we are not quite ready to go there yet. For now, let the 19th century settle around you. Let the candle light and the scratching pens and the half-built brass gears fade slowly from your mind. The river is rounding another bend. The water is moving a little faster now, not in a rush, but with a quiet sense of gathering purpose. The next part of the story is waiting, but you do not need to hurry toward it. Let your breathing stay slow. Let your body stay heavy. The ideas will keep and the story will continue whenever you are ready. The man who picked up the thread in the 20th century was not a clock maker or a poet's daughter. He was a mathematician, a long-d distanceance runner, a person who seemed to see the shape of problems before anyone else could quite make them out. His name was Alan Turing and his work forms the bridge between the paper dreams of the 19th century and the real machines that would come after. More than anyone else in this story, Turing asked the question directly, not can a machine calculate because by his time calculating machines already existed, but can a machine think? And if it can, how would we know? Alan Mat Turing was born in London in 1912. As a boy, he was curious and sometimes awkward, more interested in numbers and puzzles than in the routines of school life. He was a strong runner, almost of Olympic level later in his life, and he had a mind that did not like to take things for granted. He liked to start from first principles, to take apart a problem until he understood its smallest moving pieces, and then to build it back up again in a new and clearer form. This habit of mind would lead him in 1936 when he was just 24 years old to write a paper that changed the course of computing. The paper was called on computable numbers with an application to the nidongs problem. The title is hard to say and even harder to translate, but the idea inside it is something we can approach gently and slowly. Turing was trying to answer a deep question about mathematics itself. The question was whether there exists a step-by-step method, a definite procedure that can decide whether any given mathematical statement is true or false. To answer this question, Turing had to think very carefully about what a step-by-step method actually is. He had to think about what it means to follow a rule, to carry out a procedure, to compute something. What he came up with was an imaginary machine. It was not a machine of brass and steel. It was a machine of pure logic, something he described entirely on paper. The machine consisted of a long strip of paper tape divided into squares. Each square could hold a single symbol like a mark or a blank. The machine had a head that could read the symbol in one square at a time, and depending on what it read, and on the rules it had been given, it could erase the symbol, write a new one, and move one square to the left or one square to the right. That was it. A tape, a reading and writing head, a set of rules. Out of these very simple pieces, Turing showed that you could build up any calculation that could be done at all. If something could be computed, this little imaginary machine could compute it given enough tape and enough time. This idea is now called a touring machine. But at the time, it was just a thought experiment, a way of making the idea of a step-by-step procedure absolutely clear and precise. And the reason it matters for our story is this. Turing showed that a machine of extreme simplicity could in principle carry out any process that could be written down as a clear set of instructions. The machine did not need to understand what it was doing. It just needed to follow the rules. And if thinking or some part of thinking could be reduced to a clear set of instructions, then a machine like this could in principle carry out that part of thinking too. Turing did not say that thinking was just rule following. He simply provided a model of what a rule following machine could be and he left the deeper question hanging there for others to pick up or for himself to pick up later. Not long after he wrote this paper, the world was pulled into war. The Second World War broke out in 1939 and Touring was recruited to work at a place called Bletchley Park, a country estate in England that had been turned into a coderebreaking center. The German military was using a machine called Enigma to scramble its messages. And the Enigma codes were considered nearly unbreakable. Turing and his colleagues worked in secret in crowded wooden huts through long hours and late nights trying to find a way into the codes. Touring designed a series of electromechanical machines called bombas that helped to speed up the work of testing possible enigma settings. This was not artificial intelligence in the way we mean it now. The bombs were specialized tools for a specific job, but the work at Bletchley Park mattered for the later story in two ways. First, it showed that machines could be built to carry out logical work of enormous complexity, far faster than any human being could manage. And second, it brought Touring into direct practical contact with the reality of building machines that could process symbols according to rules. The theoretical possibility he had described in 1936 became, in the pressure of wartime, a practical necessity. After the war ended, Turing continued to think about the relationship between machines and minds. The war had shown that machines could break codes and calculate trajectories and do many things that had once seemed to require human intelligence. But could a machine actually be said to think? And if it could, how would we know? In 1950, Turing published a paper in the journal Mind, a philosophy journal with a deceptively simple opening line. He wrote, "I propose to consider the question, can machines think?" And then instead of trying to define what thinking is, which is a very hard problem that philosophers had been arguing about for centuries, he proposed a different approach. He proposed a game. The game is now called the touring test and it is one of the most famous ideas in the whole history of artificial intelligence. The setup is simple to describe. Imagine a human judge sitting at a screen typing messages back and forth with two hidden conversation partners. One of the partners is a human being, the other is a machine. The judge can ask any questions they like about any topic and the two partners will answer. After a period of conversation, the judge has to decide which partner is the human and which is the machine. If the judge cannot tell the difference reliably, if the machine can hold a conversation well enough to be mistaken for a human being, then Turing suggested, we might reasonably say that the machine is showing intelligent behavior. He did not say this would prove the machine was thinking in the deep philosophical sense. He simply offered it as a practical way of framing the question, a way that did not get tangled up in definitions of consciousness or mind or soul. Touring predicted that by the year 2000, a machine would be able to play this game well enough that an average human judge would have less than a 70% chance of correctly identifying the machine after 5 minutes of conversation. This prediction, like many predictions in the history of artificial intelligence, did not come true on the schedule he suggested. The question of whether any machine has truly passed the touring test remains a matter of debate among researchers and philosophers. Some people argue that certain modern systems have come close. Others argue that the test itself is not a good measure of intelligence because a machine can appear to converse without understanding anything at all. This is one of those places in the story where we can simply let the uncertainty sit. The test is an idea, a way of asking the question, not a final answer. Turing himself never claimed to have solved the question of machine thought. He only offered a way of asking it clearly. What matters for our story is that Turing took the abstract ideas of Bool and Babage and Love Lace and brought them into the 20th century into the age of actual electronic computers. He showed that computing was not just about numbers. It was about symbols and rules and the possibility that a machine might one day handle language and reasoning in ways that felt human. He died in 1954, just a few years after writing that paper, and he did not live to see the field he had helped to create take shape. But his ideas ran through everything that came after, like a deep underground current, shaping the questions that the next generation of researchers would ask. It is worth pausing here in the quiet of this part of the story to notice the shape of Turing's contribution. He did not build a thinking machine. He did not even try to build one. What he did was to clarify what it would mean to build one and what it would mean to say that one had succeeded. He gave the people who came after him a clear target to aim at, or at least a clear way of thinking about what the target might look like. He also gave them a rigorous model of what a computing machine could be. A model so simple and so powerful that it still underlies the theory of computation today. The touring machine is still taught in computer science courses. The touring test is still debated in philosophy seminars. The work at Bletchley Park is still studied by historians. Few people in any field have left such a deep mark with so few published papers. But the field of artificial intelligence did not yet exist as a named thing. It was still a set of ideas floating in the air. Ideas about logic and machines and the possibility of thought outside of biology. The next step in the story required someone to gather those ideas together, to give them a name, and to propose that a group of researchers spend a summer working on them together. That summer did happen a few years after Turing<unk>s death in a small town in New Hampshire. And it is to that summer and to the name that was coined there that the story will turn next. For now, though, let the figure of Alan Turing rest in your mind for a moment. Picture a man in a rumpled jacket walking through the grounds of Bletchley Park in the early morning, thinking not about the war or the codes or the machines in front of him, but about the larger question. What is thought? Can it be put into rules? Can a machine made of wires and vacuum tubes ever do more than follow instructions? He did not answer these questions. He opened them. He made them askable in a rigorous way. and the asking itself, the careful framing of the question is one of the quiet gifts he gave to the story we are following tonight. Let that gift sit there gentle and unresolved as you drift a little further towards sleep. The story will continue. The field is about to get its name, but there is no hurry. The name will still be there when you are ready for it. By the middle of the 1950s, the pieces were scattered across the table. The logic of Bool, the engines of Babage, the visions of Love Lace, the machines and questions of touring. There were electronic computers now, real ones built with vacuum tubes and wires, humming in rooms at universities and government labs. People were programming them to do mathematics, to break codes, to run simulations. But no one had yet brought all the threads together into a single focused effort. No one had said, "Let us gather the people who are curious about machine intelligence. Let us sit together for a summer. Let us see if we can make something new." That changed in the summer of 1956 in a small town in New Hampshire at a place called Dartmouth College. The man who set this in motion was a young mathematician named John McCarthy. McCarthy was born in Boston in 1927, and he had a bright, restless, far-seeing kind of mind. By the early 1950s, he was already thinking about machines that could learn and reason, and he wanted to bring together the small number of people who shared this unusual interest. He wrote a proposal, a document that he hoped would convince a funding body to support a summer workshop. The proposal was addressed to the Rockefeller Foundation and it began with a sentence that still echoes through the history of the field. It said in part that the study was to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it. Notice the careful language there. It was a conjecture, not a claim of proven fact. It was a proposal, not a report of work already done. McCarthy was saying, "Let us assume for the summer that intelligence can be broken down into steps and written into a machine. Let us see how far we can get under that assumption. This was a starting point, a working hypothesis, a way of clearing the ground so that actual research could begin. It was not a boast and it was not a promise. It was an invitation. McCarthy needed a name for this gathering and he chose one deliberately. He called it the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on artificial intelligence. This was the first known use of the term artificial intelligence in this context. McCarthy coined the phrase partly because it was clear and descriptive and partly because he wanted a name that was broad enough to hold all the different threads people were pulling on. logic, learning, language, vision, reasoning, planning. All of these could fit under the umbrella of artificial intelligence. The name stuck and it has been with us ever since. But it is worth remembering that it began as a workshop title chosen by a young man trying to describe a summer project to a foundation. It was not handed down from on high. It was a practical label, and it happened to catch on. The workshop was held in the summer of 1956 on the campus of Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. The exact dates and the exact list of attendees are matters that historians have debated a little because the workshop was not run like a modern conference with badges and registration desks and published proceedings. It was a loose gathering of about a dozen people coming and going over several weeks working in an airy room at the top of the college's mathematics building. John McCarthy was there, of course. So was Marvin Minsky, a young Harvard mathematician who would become one of the most influential figures in the field. Nathaniel Rochester, an engineer from IBM, was one of the organizers. Claude Shannon, the brilliant mathematician who had done foundational work on information theory, was there for part of the time. Other participants included Arthur Samuel, who was building a checker playing program at IBM, and Ray Solomongh, who was thinking about probability and learning, and Alan Newell and Herbert Simon, who came from the Rand Corporation and brought with them a program they had already built, a program that could prove simple logic theorems. The program that Newell and Simon brought was called the logic theorist and it is often considered one of the first working artificial intelligence programs. It could take a set of logical statements and try to find proofs for them working step by step through the rules of logic. It did not always succeed and it was limited to a very narrow kind of problem. But it was a real demonstration that a machine could do something that looked like reasoning. Newell and Simon were proud of it, and they showed it off at the workshop, and it helped to set the tone for the summer. The tone was one of optimism, of belief that big things were just around the corner, that the problems of machine intelligence might yield to sustained effort over a few years or a decade or two. The Dartmouth workshop did not produce a single breakthrough. There was no moment where everyone in the room suddenly saw the light. The work was peacemeal, exploratory, sometimes messy. People worked on different problems. Some wrote programs to play games. Some wrote programs to solve puzzles. Some talked about how a machine might understand language or recognize patterns. But the workshop did something that was perhaps more important than any single result. It created a community. It gave a group of people who had been working in isolation the sense that they were part of a shared enterprise. It gave them a name for what they were doing and it gave them the feeling that the thing they were doing was real and important and worth pursuing. After the summer ended, the participants went back to their home institutions and many of them continued to work on artificial intelligence. McCarthy moved to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and then later to Stanford where he founded one of the first artificial intelligence laboratories. Minsky also went to MIT where he became a central figure in the field for decades. Newell and Simon built on their early work and became leaders in the study of human and machine problem solving. The field began to take institutional shape. Labs were founded. Funding began to flow from government agencies, especially the Advanced Research Projects Agency known as ARPA. Conferences were organized. Journals were started. What had been a handful of scattered thinkers became within a few years a recognized academic discipline with its own journals, its own jargon, its own rising stars. But it is important to pause here and notice something about the way the field was founded. It was founded on a conjecture, a hypothesis, a hope. The proposal for the Dartmouth workshop had suggested that a significant advance could be made if a carefully selected group of scientists worked on the problem together for a summer. This was an ambitious claim and in some ways it underestimated the difficulty of the problems involved. The years that followed the workshop were full of energy and excitement and they produced real achievements. But they also produced a pattern that would repeat throughout the history of artificial intelligence. High hopes would be followed by slow progress. Bold predictions would be followed by disappointment. Summers of optimism would be followed by winters of reduced funding and diminished interest. This pattern was not yet visible in 1956. The people at Dartmouth were standing at the beginning of something, looking forward into a future that seemed wide open and full of possibility. They could not see the winters ahead. They could only see the road stretching out before them, bright and inviting. Let the image of that summer settle in your mind for a moment if you like. Picture a warm July day in New Hampshire, the trees full and green, the mathematics building quiet and a little dusty. Inside, a small group of young men in short-sleeved shirts and glasses are gathered around a blackboard, arguing about whether a machine can learn from experience, whether it needs to be told everything in advance, or whether it can figure things out on its own. The windows are open. The sound of birds comes in from outside. Someone writes a line of symbols on the board and steps back, and the others stare at it, thinking, "There is coffee and paper cups. There are papers scattered on tables. There is the low hum of an early computer somewhere down the hall. A machine the size of a refrigerator doing work that would seem laughably simple to the phone in your pocket now. But to them it was the edge of something. They could feel it. And they gave that edge a name. Artificial intelligence. A phrase that was meant to be practical and descriptive but that carried within it a whole universe of questions. What is intelligence? Can it be separated from the body, from emotion, from lived experience? Can it be built out of wires and code? Is there something about human thought that cannot be captured in rules? These questions were not answered at Dartmouth. They were not even fully asked. But the name gave people permission to ask them seriously in public with funding in students and laboratory space. The name made the field real. The story now is about to move into a period of great optimism. The late 1950s and the 1960s were a time when artificial intelligence seemed to be racing ahead. Programs were written that could play chess, solve algebra problems, even carry on simple conversations. The people building these programs made public predictions about what was coming. Human level machine intelligence within a generation. They said machines that could think truly think within a couple of decades. These predictions were made by serious people, not cranks or huers. They were made by the same people who had been at Dartmouth and by their students and colleagues. They were made in good faith based on the rapid progress of those early years. But the predictions did not come true, at least not on the timeline that was promised. The problems turned out to be much harder than they looked. The early successes were in narrow domains with simplified problems, and they did not scale up easily to the messy, complicated, open-ended problems of the real world. This gap between hope and reality would eventually lead to the first of the winters, the first of the long, cold seasons when funding dried up and interest faded and the field had to pull back and regroup. But that is a story for later. For now, in this moment of the story, it is still summer. The name is still new. The possibilities still feel endless. The first wave of optimism is just beginning to rise. And you, lying there in the dark, can let that summer warmth wash over you. The story will continue through the bright years and the cold ones, through the rises and the falls. But there is no need to rush ahead. Let the summer of 1956 hang in the air for a moment longer. A small college town, a room full of young researchers, a name written on a proposal, the beginning of something that no one in that room could fully see the end of. The river is still flowing. The current is still steady, and you are still drifting gently toward the next part of the night. The years after the Dartmouth workshop were full of light and motion. The field had a name now and it had a small but growing community of researchers and it had money beginning to flow from government agencies that were willing to bet on big ideas. The mood in those late 1950s and through the 1960s was one of extraordinary confidence. The people working on artificial intelligence believed they were at the start of something that would reshape the world. And they said so often and publicly. They made predictions that sound bold even now looking back. Human level machine intelligence within a generation. Machines that could translate languages, understand speech, recognize objects, reason about the world. These predictions were not made by fringe figures. They were made by the leaders of the field, the same people who had been at Dartmouth or who had joined the effort soon after. And for a while, the early results seemed to back them up. One of the first real landmarks of this period was a machine called the perceptron built by a psychologist named Frank Rosenblat. Rosenblat worked at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York. And in the late 1950s, he designed a device that was meant to learn in a way that was loosely inspired by the brain. The brain, as scientists had known for some time, is made up of billions of tiny cells called neurons connected to one another in vast complicated networks. Each neuron receives signals from its neighbors, and if the signals are strong enough, it fires a signal of its own. Rosenblat wanted to build a very simple version of this idea in hardware. His perceptron was a machine made of wires and resistors and motors with a grid of 400 light sensors arranged in a square. It could be shown simple patterns like letters of the alphabet, and it could learn to tell them apart. It did this by adjusting the strength of the connections between its parts, making some pathways stronger and some weaker until the correct output was produced more and more reliably. This idea of a system that adjusts itself based on examples rather than being given exact rules in advance is a very important idea in the history of artificial intelligence. It is a form of machine learning which is the broader term for systems that improve their performance by being shown data rather than being programmed with every step spelled out. The perceptron was an early simple version of what would later be called a neural network, a computing system built from many small connected units that work together to recognize patterns. At the time, the perceptron caused a great deal of excitement. The New York Times wrote about it. People speculated about what it might lead to. Rosenblat himself was optimistic and he gave interviews in which he talked about machines that would one day read and speak and even become conscious. But the perceptron had limits and those limits would become important later in the story. For now, in the warm glow of the early years, what mattered was that a machine had shown it could learn even in a simple way. It was not following a fixed set of instructions written by a programmer. It was adjusting itself, getting better with practice in a way that felt almost biological. That sense of the biological, of machines edging closer to something lielike, was very much in the air. Another sign of that feeling was a program called Eliza, written in 1966 by a computer scientist named Joseph Weisenbomb at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Eliza was a conversation program, one of the first programs designed to interact with a person in plain written language. Weisenbomb gave Eliza a particular role to play. The program was scripted to act like a psychotherapist of a certain kind, the kind who listens to what a patient says and responds by reflecting it back in a slightly different form. If you typed, "I am feeling sad," Eliza might respond, why do you say you are feeling sad? If you typed, "My mother is difficult," Eliza might ask, "Tell me more about your mother." The program was not thinking. It was following a set of simple rules for taking the words a person typed and rearranging them into a question or a prompt. It had no understanding of sadness, no knowledge of mothers, no inner life at all. It was a set of text manipulation tricks. But the effect on people who used it was striking. Some users became emotionally involved with Eliza. They treated it as if it were a real listener, a real presence on the other side of the screen. Widesenbomb himself was disturbed by this. He had not intended to build something that people would form attachments to. He had only wanted to show how easy it was to create a surface illusion of conversation. The Eliza effect, as it later came to be called, became a recurring theme in the story of artificial intelligence. It refers to the human tendency to attribute understanding and feeling to machines that are simply following rules, especially when those machines use language in a way that feels familiar. Eliza was not intelligent, but it was the first of many programs that would raise the question of whether seeming intelligent is the same as being intelligent and whether the difference matters. Around the same time, another kind of project was taking shape. One that moved the question of intelligence from words on a screen to physical movement in the real world. At the Stanford Research Institute in California, a team of engineers built a robot they named Shaky. Shaky was not a human-shaped robot. It was a tall box on wheels with a camera and a set of sensors connected to a computer that filled an entire room. But Shaky could do something that no robot had done before. It could reason about its own actions. It could be given a goal, like push the block off the platform, and it could figure out a sequence of steps to achieve that goal, moving around obstacles, adjusting its plan if something changed. This required a combination of skills. Shaki had to build an internal model of its environment to understand where things were and how they related to one another. It had to plan a series of actions and it had to check its progress and revise its plan if things did not go as expected. The researchers who built Shaki gave it a set of programs for solving problems by breaking them down into smaller pieces. A technique that came to be known as means ends analysis. The system would look at the difference between where it was and where it wanted to be and then find an action that would reduce that difference and then repeat the process until the goal was reached. This was slow work. The computer Shaky was connected to was not fast by modern standards. A single action might take minutes or hours to plan and execute. But the point was not speed. The point was that a machine was demonstrating something that looked very much like deliberation, a step-by-step process of thinking about what to do. Shaki was one of the first systems to combine perception, planning, and action in a single working robot and it helped to establish the field that is now called robotics. These three projects, the perceptron, Eliza and Shaky were quite different from one another. One was about learning from examples. One was about processing language. One was about planning and moving in physical space. But together they gave the sense that artificial intelligence was advancing on many fronts at once. If a machine could learn to recognize patterns and hold a conversation and reason about its own actions, then surely a machine that could do all of these things together was only a matter of time. Or so the thinking went. The funding agencies agreed, or at least they were willing to bet on the possibility. The Advanced Research Projects Agency, known as ARPA, poured millions of dollars into artificial intelligence research at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Melon, and other universities. The money paid for computer time, which was expensive in those days. It paid for graduate students. It paid for laboratories. It created an environment in which smart people could work on hard problems without having to justify every short-term result. The assumption was that the big results were coming and that patience would be rewarded and the predictions kept coming too. Herbert Simon, one of the central figures in the field said in 1965 that machines would be capable within 20 years of doing any work a man can do. Marvin Minsky told an interviewer in 1970 that a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being would probably exist within 3 to 8 years. These were not casual remarks. They were statements made by people at the top of the field, people whose opinions carried weight with funders and journalists and the public. They were made in good faith based on the rapid pace of early progress. But they were wrong. The timeline they imagined turned out to be off by decades and in some cases by more than half a century. The problems that looked simple, like understanding a sentence or recognizing a face in a photograph, turned out to be deeply hard. The problems that looked hard, like playing chess, turned out to be solvable in unexpected ways. But the solvable ones were not enough to build a general intelligence. And the hard ones stayed hard for much longer than anyone expected. It is easy looking back to see the overconfidence of those early years. But it is also worth understanding where it came from. The researchers of the 1960s were working with computers that were by modern standards almost impossibly limited. They had less memory than a pocket calculator has today. They had less processing power than a musical greeting card. And yet on these tiny, slow, primitive machines, they had managed to build programs that could do things that looked astonishing at the time. A machine that could learn, a machine that could converse, a machine that could plan. If they could do that much with so little, what would they be able to do when computers got faster and bigger and cheaper as everyone knew they would? The logic was not unreasonable. It was simply that the difficulty of the problems did not scale in the way the researchers expected. Some things that are easy for a human brain because the brain has been shaped by millions of years of evolution to do them are extraordinarily difficult for a machine. Recognizing a face, understanding a joke, walking across a room without falling over. These things require vast amounts of unconscious computation that the brain does without effort but that a computer has to be taught from scratch. The early optimism was not foolish. It was human. It was the optimism of explorers who had just landed on a new shore and believed the interior of the continent was only a few days walk away. They could not see the mountains and the deserts and the long rivers that lay between them and the far coast. They could only see what was in front of them. And what was in front of them was new and bright and full of promise. But the mountains were there. The limits of the early approaches were real, and they were about to become harder to ignore. The researchers are still full of hope. The money is still flowing. The summer of the field's youth is still in full bloom. Let that bloom linger in your mind for a moment. Let the warm years fade softly. The next part of the night is waiting. The warm years did not end all at once. There was no single day when the money stopped or the lights went out. What happened was slower than that and quieter. A gradual cooling that settled over the field of artificial intelligence across the late 1960s and into the 1970s. The big predictions kept not coming true. The problems that had looked simple turned out to be stubborn and deep. And the people who controlled the funding in governments and universities and military agencies began to ask harder questions about what they were getting for their money. The season that followed has come to be called an artificial intelligence winter. It is a phrase worth understanding calmly because it will appear more than once in this story. A winter in this context is not a disaster. It is not a crash. It is a period when the warmth of funding and public attention pulls back. When the field contracts, when many researchers leave or shift to other problems, and when the ones who stay do so quietly, keeping the embers alive until conditions change. The first of these winters arrived in the 1970s, and it came from several directions at once. One of the earliest signs of the coming cold was a book published in 1969. The book was called Perceptrons and it was written by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert, two of the most respected figures in artificial intelligence. Minsky, as you may remember, had been one of the organizers of the Dartmouth workshop. He was a brilliant forceful thinker and when he spoke, people listened. In perceptrons, Minsky and Papert laid out a careful mathematical analysis of what the simple perceptron networks like the one Frank Rosenblat had built could and could not do. They showed that a single layer of perceptron-like units had strict limits. It could learn to recognize patterns that were linearly separable, which is a technical way of saying that you could draw a straight line through the data and put all the examples of one kind on one side and all the examples of the other kind on the other side. But many real world problems are not that simple. A perceptron could not learn to tell whether a pattern of black and white dots was connected or not. It could not solve certain basic logical puzzles. These were fundamental limits, not just engineering problems that could be solved with faster hardware or more data. The book was rigorous and influential, and it had a chilling effect on research into neural networks, the kind of learning systems that Rosenlat had championed. Funding for that line of work dried up. Graduate students were steered away from it. The whole approach went into a kind of hibernation that lasted for more than a decade. It is worth noting that Minsky and Paper were not trying to kill the field. They were trying to clarify what the simple models could do and they acknowledged in the book that more complex networks with multiple layers might overcome the limits they had identified. But the practical effect of the book was to cast a shadow over neural network research and that shadow was long and cold. Rosenblat himself died in a boating accident in 1971 and with his death the field lost one of its most passionate advocates for this approach. The chill from perceptrons was largely about one particular research direction within artificial intelligence. But a broader chill was coming and it was driven by a more general sense that the field as a whole had overpromised and underdelivered. The predictions made in the 1960s about machines that would match human intelligence within a generation had not come true. And they were not looking any closer to coming true. As the 1970s began, machine translation, which had received a great deal of funding, was producing results that were clumsy and unreliable. Speech recognition was barely working. Computer vision was in its infancy. The grand ambitions of the early years had run into the hard reality that many aspects of intelligence are extraordinarily difficult to replicate in a machine. This growing skepticism found its most influential expression in a report published in 1973 commissioned by the British government and written by a mathematician named Sir James Lighill. The report was formerly titled artificial intelligence a general survey but it is nearly always referred to as the lighill report. Lighill had been asked by the science research council the main government funding body for science in the United Kingdom to evaluate the state of artificial intelligence research in the country and to advise on whether it deserved continued public support. Lighill was an outsider to the field. He was a respected applied mathematician, a person who had made real contributions to fluid dynamics and other areas and he approached the question with a skeptical eye. He read the papers, he visited the labs, he talked to the researchers and then he wrote a report that was sharply critical of much of what he had seen. The Ligh report divided artificial intelligence research into three rough categories. Category A was what he called advanced automation. Things like pattern recognition and control systems which he thought were useful but not really about intelligence. Category C was research on the central nervous system including computer models of the brain which he thought was interesting science but belonged in biology and psychology departments not in computing. Category B was the core of artificial intelligence, the attempt to build machines that could reason and solve problems in general ways. And it was category B that Lighill criticized most heavily. He argued that the field had made far less progress than its proponents claimed, that its successes were largely in toy problems that did not scale up to real world complexity, and that there was no good reason to believe that the approaches being pursued would lead to general machine intelligence anytime soon, if ever. The report had consequences. The British government, acting on Lighill's recommendations, drastically reduced its funding for artificial intelligence research. The cuts were deep enough that several research groups in the United Kingdom were disbanded or had to shrink to a fraction of their former size. The effects rippled outward. The United States, which had been the largest funer of artificial intelligence research through ARPA, began to tighten its own support. The United States Congress passed the Mansfield Amendment in 1970, which required that defense funded research be directly relevant to military applications. Artificial intelligence research had often been funded under the broad umbrella of basic science, but now it had to justify itself in more concrete terms. ARPA, which had been generous and patient, began to ask harder questions about deliverables and timelines. The money did not disappear completely, but it shrank, and the mood shifted from one of expansive optimism to one of cautious, sometimes defensive justification. This is the period that historians of the field now refer to as the first artificial intelligence winter. The term is a metaphor of course. There was no snow, no ice, no frozen ground. It was a winter of the spirit, a season of reduced resources and diminished expectations. But it is important not to exaggerate the cold. Work did not stop. Researchers still went to their labs. Papers were still published. Conferences were still held. The winter was not a complete shutdown.
